title: Hereditary and Productive Behaviour of the Separation Axioms

items.title: $T_0$, $T_1$, and Hausdorffness are hereditary
items.strategy: Intersect the distinguishing or separating open sets with the subspace and use the trace description of closure for the $T_1$ formulation.

items.title: Regularity is hereditary, without a hidden $T_1$ hypothesis
items.strategy: Use the closed-neighbourhood characterization: trace an ambient closed neighbourhood down to the subspace.

items.title: Complete regularity is hereditary, without a hidden $T_1$ hypothesis
items.strategy: Lift a subspace-closed set to an ambient closed set and restrict the separating continuous function.

items.title: $T_0$, $T_1$, $T_2$, regularity, $T_3$, complete regularity, and Tychonoffness are hereditary
items.strategy: Assemble the three structural lemmas, adding $T_1$ exactly where the library's $T_3$ and Tychonoff conventions require it.

items.title: Arbitrary products preserve $T_0$, $T_1$, and Hausdorffness
items.strategy: Separate two unequal tuples in a coordinate where they differ and pull the relevant open sets back along that projection; treat the empty product explicitly.

items.title: Arbitrary products of regular spaces are regular
items.strategy: Shrink each of the finitely many active coordinates of a basic neighbourhood and take the corresponding finite-support product neighbourhood.

items.title: Finite pointwise minima of continuous maps to $[0,1]$ are continuous
items.strategy: Prove the binary minimum map continuous by computing preimages of open rays in the product topology, then induct over a finite family; the empty minimum is the constant-one map.

items.title: Arbitrary products of completely regular spaces are completely regular
items.strategy: Place a finite-support basic neighbourhood inside the complement of the closed set, separate in each active coordinate, and combine the finitely many coordinate functions by a continuous minimum.

items.title: $T_0$, $T_1$, $T_2$, regularity, $T_3$, complete regularity, and Tychonoffness are productive
items.strategy: Combine the coordinate and finite-support lemmas, again adding $T_1$ only for the named compound axioms.

items.title: Every closed subspace of a normal space is normal
items.strategy: Regard two disjoint closed subsets of the closed subspace as disjoint ambient closed sets and trace ambient separating neighbourhoods.

items.title: A space is completely normal if and only if every subspace is normal
items.strategy: For the forward direction, turn two subspace-closed sets into separated ambient sets and use complete normality. For the reverse direction, place two separated sets in their union, where each is closed, and lift the separating subspace opens.

items.title: Complete normality, and hence $T_5$, is hereditary
items.strategy: A subspace of a hereditarily normal space is again hereditarily normal; preserve $T_1$ separately.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, perfect normality, and hence $T_6$, is hereditary
items.strategy: Use perfect normality to obtain complete normality, then intersect the ambient $G_\delta$ representation of a closed lift with the subspace.

items.title: Every regular Lindelöf space is normal
items.strategy: Shrink point neighbourhoods of one closed set away from the other, thin the resulting cover countably, and separate by the union of the shrunken opens from the complement of their closures.

items.title: The lower-limit topology on $\mathbb{R}$, with the half-open intervals $[a,b)$ as a basis
The lower-limit line has a clopen basis, is regular, and is Lindelöf under countable choice
items.strategy: Check half-open intervals are clopen, then thin an arbitrary basic refinement using rational endpoints plus the countable exceptional set left by the corresponding Euclidean open union.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, the lower-limit line is normal
items.strategy: Apply regular plus Lindelöf implies normal.

items.title: Jones's bound: under choice, a closed discrete subspace of a normal space cannot have more subsets than a dense set has subsets
items.strategy: For each subset of the closed discrete set choose a normal separation from its complement; its intersection with the dense set determines the subset, giving an injection between the two power sets.

items.title: The lower-limit plane has a countable dense set and a closed discrete antidiagonal of size $|\mathbb{R}|$
items.strategy: Use rational points in every basic rectangle; isolate each antidiagonal point with a half-open rectangle and separate every off-antidiagonal point by a rectangle on which the coordinate sum has fixed sign.

items.title: Assuming choice, normality is not productive: the normal lower-limit line has a nonnormal square
items.strategy: Apply Jones's bound to the countable dense set and continuum-sized closed discrete antidiagonal. Reconstruct locally the ZF equinumerosity $\mathbb{R}\approx\mathcal P(\mathbb N)$, since its published worked item is on a B page, and contradict Cantor's theorem.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, the deleted Tychonoff plank is a regular nonnormal open subspace of a compact Hausdorff normal space
items.strategy: Use ordinal $T_3$-ness and productive regularity for the deleted plank, Tychonoff compactness plus compact Hausdorff normality for the full plank, and separate the two edge sets only far enough to derive the standard boundedness contradiction below $\omega_1$.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, normality is not hereditary, even to open regular subspaces
items.strategy: Use the full Tychonoff plank and its deleted open subspace from the preceding lemma.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, refuted: every regular space is normal
items.strategy: The deleted Tychonoff plank is the licensed regular nonnormal witness.

items.title: Preservation ledger for the separation axioms, with $T_1$ conventions kept explicit
A worked preservation table for subspaces and products of the standard, cofinite, and ordinal topologies
items.strategy: Check representative rows directly and use the A-page preservation theorems for the general columns.

items.title: Closed subspaces inherit normality: compact intervals, ordinal endpoints, and finite closed pieces
items.strategy: Identify each subset as closed and apply closed-heredity, noting that no conclusion is available for an arbitrary subspace.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, the deleted Tychonoff plank worked as $T_3$ but not normal inside its compact Hausdorff normal parent
items.strategy: Compute the edge sets and the tail rectangles explicitly, isolating the one use of countable boundedness below $\omega_1$.

items.title: Assuming choice, the lower-limit line is normal while its square is regular and nonnormal
items.strategy: Display the clopen interval base, the finite-support product base, and the Jones antidiagonal obstruction side by side.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, normality is not open-hereditary: deleting one corner of the Tychonoff plank
items.strategy: The deleted corner is closed, so its complement is open; the A-page lemma supplies normality of the parent and nonnormality of the complement.

items.title: Assuming choice, normality is not even finitely productive: two copies of the lower-limit line
items.strategy: Package the square theorem as the sharp binary counterexample.

items.title: Regular and normal do not imply $T_1$ under the library's conventions
items.strategy: Use a small indiscrete space, where the relevant point-versus-closed-set and closed-set-versus-closed-set obligations are vacuous but $T_1$ fails.

items.title: Refinements, locally finite families, point-finite families, and star refinements
Locally finite families remain locally finite after taking closures, closure commutes with their union, and a locally finite union of closed sets is closed
items.strategy: At a point choose one neighbourhood meeting only finitely many members; the same neighbourhood misses the closures of every other member.

items.title: Paracompactness: every open cover has a locally finite open refinement, with no separation axiom built into the word
Every compact space is paracompact
items.strategy: A finite subcover is itself a finite, hence locally finite, open refinement.

items.title: Every closed subspace of a paracompact space is paracompact
items.strategy: Extend a subspace cover to the ambient space by adjoining the complement of the closed subspace, refine there, and take traces.

items.title: Every paracompact Hausdorff space is regular
items.strategy: For a point outside a closed set, take all Hausdorff neighbourhoods of closed-set points whose closures miss the point, refine this cover locally finitely, and unite the refinement members that meet the closed set; local finiteness lets closure commute with that union and keeps the point out, with no simultaneous choice of neighbourhoods.

items.title: Every paracompact Hausdorff space is normal
items.strategy: Use the preceding regularity result to take the family of all neighbourhoods of one closed set whose closures miss the other, refine the resulting cover locally finitely, and unite just the refinement members meeting that closed set.

items.title: Locally finite partitions of unity and subordination to an open cover
Sums, products, absolute values, finite maxima and minima, and quotients of continuous real-valued maps on a topological space are continuous where defined
items.strategy: Pair the maps into $\mathbb R^2$ by the product universal property and prove the elementary real operations continuous by epsilon estimates; compose, restricting a quotient to the open cozero set of its denominator.

items.title: A locally finite family of continuous nonnegative functions has a continuous pointwise sum
items.strategy: Near each point all but finitely many functions vanish, so the pointwise sum agrees locally with a finite continuous sum.

items.title: A locally finite nonnegative family with positive pointwise sum normalizes to a partition of unity
items.strategy: Apply the locally finite sum lemma and divide every function by the everywhere-positive sum; supports and local finiteness are unchanged.

items.title: Under choice, every open cover of a paracompact Hausdorff space has locally finite open refinements $\{V_s\}$ and $\{W_s\}$ with $\overline{V_s}\subseteq W_s\subseteq U_s$
items.strategy: Use regularity to shrink one neighbourhood at each point inside an assigned refinement member, then invoke paracompactness a second time; local finiteness makes the closures of the second refinement stay inside the first assigned members.

items.title: Under choice and dependent choice, every open cover of a paracompact Hausdorff space admits a locally finite subordinate partition of unity
items.strategy: Shrink the cover twice, apply Urysohn's lemma to each pair $\overline{V_s}\subseteq W_s$, and normalize the resulting locally finite positive family.

items.title: For a Hausdorff space, paracompactness is equivalent, under choice and dependent choice, to the existence of a locally finite subordinate partition of unity for every open cover
items.strategy: Use the existence theorem forward; conversely the positive cozero sets of a subordinate partition form a locally finite open refinement.

items.title: Under choice and dependent choice, every open cover of a compact Hausdorff space admits a finite subordinate partition of unity
items.strategy: Use compactness for a finite subcover and the partition theorem, then group all functions assigned to the same member of that finite subcover; local finiteness makes each grouped sum continuous.

items.title: Under choice, every open cover of a metric space has a point-finite open refinement
items.strategy: Following Ornstein's first stage, stratify points by a dyadic ball small enough to lie in a cover member, well-order each stratum, and retain only the first eligible balls; verify point-finiteness scale by scale.

items.title: Under choice, Ornstein's point-finite refinement of a metric cover admits a locally finite open refinement
items.strategy: Following Ornstein's second stage, assign controlled dyadic radii relative to the finitely many cover members through each point and peel successive closed cores; the metric estimates give a neighbourhood meeting only finitely many retained sets.

items.title: Stone's theorem, under choice: every metric space is paracompact
items.strategy: Apply the point-finite refinement lemma and then its locally finite upgrade to an arbitrary metric open cover.

items.title: Under choice and dependent choice, metric open covers admit locally finite subordinate partitions of unity
items.strategy: Metric spaces are Hausdorff, then apply Stone and the partition theorem.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, every countably compact paracompact Hausdorff space is compact
items.strategy: A locally finite open refinement of an open cover cannot have infinitely many essential members in a countably compact space; a finite selection of their assigned cover members is then a subcover.

items.title: Under countable choice, every regular Lindelöf space is paracompact
items.strategy: Shrink an all-eligible-neighbourhood refinement and thin it to a countable cover; replacing its enumeration by successive differences of accumulated closed cores yields a locally finite open refinement.

items.title: Refuted: every paracompact space is normal
items.strategy: Use a finite compact topology with two disjoint closed sets that have no disjoint open neighbourhoods; compactness gives paracompactness, while the failure shows why Hausdorffness is load-bearing.

items.title: Refuted: paracompactness is hereditary
items.strategy: The compact ordinal $\omega_1+1$ is paracompact, while its open subspace $\omega_1$ is countably compact and noncompact and hence not paracompact by the preceding lemma.

items.title: Assuming choice, refuted: paracompactness is productive
items.strategy: The lower-limit line is regular Lindelöf and therefore paracompact. Its square is Hausdorff but nonnormal by the earlier preservation page, so paracompact Hausdorff implies normal rules out paracompactness.

items.title: Choice and convention ledger for paracompactness, Stone's theorem, and partitions of unity

title: Partitions of Unity and Paracompactness Examples

items.title: A locally finite hat-function partition of unity on $\mathbb{R}$ subordinate to overlapping unit intervals
items.strategy: Write the piecewise-linear translates explicitly, verify only two are nonzero at each point, and compute their sum as one.

items.title: Under choice and dependent choice, a finite subordinate partition of unity for a two-set cover of a compact interval
items.strategy: Use one explicit cutoff function and its complement, then compare the construction with the compact Hausdorff existence theorem.

items.title: Point-finite need not mean locally finite: intervals accumulating at the origin
items.strategy: Give an explicit family in $\mathbb{R}$ whose every point lies in finitely many members but every neighbourhood of the origin meets infinitely many.

items.title: Without local finiteness, a pointwise finite sum of continuous functions can be discontinuous
items.strategy: Use narrow triangular bumps accumulating at the origin, with disjoint supports away from the origin and heights bounded away from zero.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, $\omega_1$ is countably compact, noncompact, and not paracompact
items.strategy: Combine the published ordinal compactness computation with countably compact plus paracompact Hausdorff implies compact.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, paracompactness is not open-hereditary: $\omega_1$ inside $\omega_1+1$
items.strategy: The successor ordinal is compact and hence paracompact, while its open initial segment is the preceding nonparacompact example.

items.title: Assuming choice, two paracompact lower-limit lines can have a nonparacompact product
items.strategy: Expand the locally reconstructed lower-limit witness from the A-page and isolate the failure of Lindelöfness in the antidiagonal.

items.title: Second countability: an at most countable basis for the topology
Separability: the existence of an at most countable dense subset
The countable chain condition: every pairwise-disjoint family of nonempty open sets is at most countable
Under choice, weight $w(X)$, density $d(X)$, local character $\chi(x,X)$, and character $\chi(X)$ as raw cardinal minima and a supremum
Under choice, Lindelöf degree $L(X)$ and cellularity $c(X)$ as raw cardinal functions
Under choice, $w(X)$ is a well-defined cardinal
items.strategy: The topology itself is a basis, so the nonempty set of cardinalities of bases has a least member.

items.title: Under choice, $d(X)$ is a well-defined cardinal
items.strategy: The whole space is dense in itself, so the cardinalities of dense subsets form a nonempty set of cardinals and have a least member.

items.title: Under choice, $\chi(x,X)$ and $\chi(X)$ are well-defined cardinals
items.strategy: The neighbourhood filter is a local base; take the least local-base cardinal at each point and the cardinal supremum over the resulting set.

items.title: Under choice, $L(X)$ is a well-defined cardinal
items.strategy: Every open cover is a subfamily of the topology and is itself a subcover, so one cardinal bound works; take the least working cardinal.

items.title: Under choice, $c(X)$ is a well-defined cardinal
items.strategy: Every disjoint family of nonempty open sets is a subfamily of the topology, so its cardinality is bounded; take the supremum of the resulting set of cardinals.

items.title: Under choice, the five cardinal functions recover first countability, second countability, separability, Lindelöfness, and ccc at the $\aleph_0$ threshold
items.strategy: Unpack the five definitions, using the library's convention that countable means at most countable.

items.title: A countable local base can be chosen open and decreasing
items.strategy: Extract the construction already used in the published sequence theorem: enumerate the base, replace members by open neighbourhoods, and take running finite intersections.

items.title: Every second countable space is first countable
items.strategy: At a point retain the members of a global countable basis that contain it.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, every second countable space is separable
items.strategy: Choose one point from each nonempty member of a countable basis; the chosen set meets every nonempty basic open set.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, every second countable space is Lindelöf
items.strategy: For each basis member lying inside a member of the cover, choose one such cover member; the selected countable family covers.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, a metrizable space is second countable if and only if it is separable if and only if it is Lindelöf
items.strategy: Use rational-radius balls around a countable dense set for separable implies second countable, the general second-countable implication, and countable subcovers of the radius-$1/n$ ball covers for Lindelöf implies separable.

items.title: Second countability is hereditary
items.strategy: Take traces of a countable ambient basis.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, a countable product of second countable spaces is second countable
items.strategy: Choose a countable basis in each factor and enumerate the finite-support boxes using countable unions of finite products of countable sets.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, a countable product of first countable spaces is first countable
items.strategy: At a point enumerate finite-support products of chosen countable local bases.

items.title: Every separable space satisfies the countable chain condition
items.strategy: Enumerate a countable dense set and assign to each disjoint nonempty open set the least enumerated point it contains; disjointness makes the assignment injective.

items.title: Under choice, $c(X)\le d(X)\le w(X)$ and $\chi(X),L(X)\le w(X)$
items.strategy: Choose a point from each nonempty basis element for density; assign a least dense point to each disjoint open set; obtain local bases by restriction and cover subfamilies by choosing one cover member above each eligible basis element.

items.title: Under choice, for $Y\subseteq X$, $w(Y)\le w(X)$ and $\chi(y,Y)\le\chi(y,X)$
items.strategy: Trace a basis and local bases to the subspace.

items.title: Under choice, a continuous surjection does not increase density or Lindelöf degree
items.strategy: The image of a dense set is dense under a surjection, and an open cover of the codomain pulls back to one of the domain.

items.title: Under choice, every metrizable space has $w(X)=d(X)$
items.strategy: The basic inequality gives $d\le w$; rational-radius balls around a least dense set give $w\le d$ for infinite density, while the finite case is discrete and checked separately.

items.title: Under choice, the uncountable $\Delta$-system lemma for finite sets
items.strategy: Thin to a fixed finite size, induct on that size, and use the uncountable pigeonhole split according to whether one point occurs uncountably often.

items.title: Under choice, every Cantor cube $2^I$ satisfies ccc
items.strategy: An uncountable family of basic cylinders has finite supports; thin the supports to a delta system and then thin again so the finitely many root coordinates carry one common pattern, forcing two cylinders to meet.

items.title: Under choice, if $|I|>2^{\aleph_0}$, then the Cantor cube $2^I$ is not separable
items.strategy: A countable set of points induces at most $2^{\aleph_0}$ coordinate columns; two equal columns leave a two-coordinate basic cylinder disjoint from the alleged dense set.

items.title: Assuming choice, refuted: every ccc space is separable
items.strategy: Take a Cantor cube indexed by a cardinal strictly above $2^{\aleph_0}$.

items.title: Refuted: every first countable space is second countable
items.strategy: Use an uncountable discrete space: singleton local bases give first countability, while every global basis must contain every singleton.

items.title: Refuted: every separable space is second countable
items.strategy: Construct the lower-limit line locally, use the rationals for separability, and inject the reals into any basis by choosing a basis member whose left endpoint is forced at each point.

items.title: Refuted: separability is hereditary
items.strategy: Construct the lower-limit plane locally: its rational grid is dense, while its uncountable discrete antidiagonal has no proper dense subset.

items.title: Refuted: Lindelöfness is hereditary
items.strategy: Take the one-point compactification of an uncountable discrete space; the whole space is compact while the open discrete subspace is not Lindelöf.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, refuted: Lindelöfness is productive
items.strategy: Rebuild the lower-limit line: thin covers by rational intervals to prove it Lindelöf, then use the closed uncountable discrete antidiagonal to show its square is not.

items.title: Assuming choice and countable choice, refuted: arbitrary products of second countable spaces are second countable
items.strategy: A sufficiently large Cantor cube has second countable two-point factors but is not separable, whereas second countability would imply separability under countable choice.

items.title: Implication, preservation, counterexample, and choice ledger for the countability axioms

title: Countability Axioms and Cardinal Functions Examples

items.title: Under choice, for the usual real line, $w=d=\chi=L=c=\aleph_0$ under the raw convention
items.strategy: Use rational intervals and rational points for the upper bounds, then rule out finite bases, dense sets, and local bases and exhibit arbitrarily large finite disjoint open families and covers.

items.title: Under choice, for an infinite discrete space of cardinality $\kappa$, $w=d=L=c=\kappa$ while $\chi=1$
items.strategy: Singletons force the basis, dense set, and cellular family; the singleton at a point is a one-member local base, and the singleton cover forces the Lindelöf degree.

items.title: For the lower-limit line, $\chi=d=L=c=\aleph_0$ and $w=2^{\aleph_0}$ under choice
items.strategy: Reconstruct the half-open basis, use rational density and the Lindelöf thinning argument, force distinct basis members at distinct left endpoints, and bound disjoint open families by density.

items.title: Assuming choice, the lower-limit plane is first countable, separable, and ccc, but not second countable or Lindelöf
items.strategy: Use product local bases and the rational grid, inherit ccc from separability, and use the uncountable closed discrete antidiagonal for the two failures.

items.title: The one-point compactification of an uncountable discrete space is compact and Lindelöf but need not be first countable or separable
items.strategy: Neighbourhoods of infinity have finite complements; a countable local base would make the discrete part countable, and density must contain every isolated point.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, $\omega_1$ is first countable and countably compact but is not separable or Lindelöf
items.strategy: Build countable cofinal local bases below each countable ordinal, then use boundedness of countable subsets and the standard initial-segment cover.

items.title: Under choice, a concrete ccc nonseparable Cantor cube indexed above $2^{\aleph_0}$
items.strategy: Take the index set to be a power set of a set of size $2^{\aleph_0}$ and apply the delta-system ccc theorem and repeated-column nonseparability lemma.

items.title: Assuming choice, a separable space with a nonseparable subspace: the lower-limit plane and its antidiagonal
items.strategy: Expand the rectangle calculation showing the rational grid is dense and every antidiagonal singleton is subspace-open.

items.title: Assuming choice, a Lindelöf space whose square is not Lindelöf: the lower-limit line
items.strategy: Expand the rational-endpoint cover thinning in the factor and the closed-discrete obstruction in the square.
